title: Classes
summary: A **class** is a template for creating objects with shared methods and per-instance data. JavaScript classes are clean syntax over the prototype system — `class` looks object-oriented, but under the hood it still uses constructor functions and prototypes.

subtopics.title: Class syntax and the constructor
subtopics.explanation: A class declaration defines a blueprint. The special constructor method runs when you create an instance with `new`, receiving the arguments and initializing instance properties via `this`. A class can have at most one constructor; if you omit it, an empty one is supplied.

subtopics.title: Instance methods
subtopics.explanation: Methods declared in the class body (without `function`) are placed on the class's prototype, so every instance shares one copy rather than each getting its own function. They access instance data through `this`.

subtopics.title: extends and super
subtopics.explanation: `extends` makes one class inherit from another, linking their prototypes. In a subclass constructor you must call super(...) before using `this` — it runs the parent constructor. super.method() calls the parent's version of an overridden method.

subtopics.title: Static members
subtopics.explanation: Static methods and fields belong to the class itself, not to instances. They're called on the class (User.create()) and are useful for factory functions, utilities, and shared constants that don't depend on a particular instance.

subtopics.title: Getters and setters
subtopics.explanation: get and set define accessor properties: code that runs when a property is read or assigned, while still looking like a plain property to callers. They're ideal for computed values and validation on assignment.

subtopics.title: Private fields (#)
subtopics.explanation: Fields prefixed with # are truly private — accessible only inside the class body and inaccessible (even un-detectable) from outside. This gives real encapsulation without closures, replacing the old underscore convention with a language-enforced boundary.

subtopics.title: Classes are prototype sugar
subtopics.explanation: Despite the OOP appearance, a class is still a function: typeof MyClass === 'function'. Methods live on MyClass.prototype, instances delegate to it, and extends wires the prototype chain. Understanding this demystifies class behavior and bridges to the prototype model.

subtopics.title: instanceof
subtopics.explanation: instanceof checks whether a constructor's prototype appears anywhere in an object's prototype chain — i.e., whether the object was created by that class or a subclass. It's the standard way to test an object's type within a hierarchy.

foundations.overview: Classes give JavaScript a familiar, readable way to define object types with constructors, shared methods, inheritance, and encapsulation. Introduced in ES2015 (with private fields and static blocks added later), they standardize patterns that developers previously hand-wrote with constructor functions and prototypes.
foundations.formalDefinition: A class is a special function that serves as a template for creating objects. Its body defines a constructor (run on instantiation), prototype methods shared by all instances, static members on the class itself, and optionally private fields enforced by the language.
foundations.whyItMatters: Classes are the idiomatic way to model entities (User, Order, Component) with shared behavior and state. They're widely used in frameworks, libraries, and OOP-style codebases, and interviewers expect you to know both the syntax and that it's prototype-based underneath.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a class as a cookie cutter: the class is the cutter (the shared shape and behavior), and each `new` call stamps out a cookie (an instance) that carries its own data but shares the cutter's design.
foundations.browserPerspective: The engine treats a class as a constructor function whose methods live on its prototype. instanceof and method calls go through the same prototype-chain lookups as constructor functions; class bodies run in strict mode automatically.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Modeling domain entities, building React class components (legacy), defining custom errors (class AppError extends Error), and structuring services and stores in OOP-leaning codebases.
foundations.businessImpact: Clear class hierarchies make domain logic easier to read and extend, reducing onboarding time and bugs in business-critical models like billing or user accounts.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Classes provide encapsulation (private fields), polymorphism (method overriding), and a consistent structure, but over-deep inheritance can create rigid designs — composition is often preferable.
foundations.performanceImpact: Methods on the prototype are shared across instances, so classes are memory-efficient. Private fields and consistent shapes keep engines on optimized paths; creating instances is comparable to constructor functions.
commonUseCases: Modeling domain entities with shared methods (User, Product, Order)
Custom error types: class ValidationError extends Error
Encapsulating internal state with private # fields and getters/setters

commonMisconceptions.myth: JavaScript classes are a different mechanism from prototypes.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A class is syntactic sugar over constructor functions and prototypes — typeof Class is 'function' and methods live on Class.prototype.
They're private only by convention and are fully accessible; true privacy requires # private fields, which the language enforces.

visualExplorer.title: What happens when you `new` a subclass
visualExplorer.caption: Step through constructing a Dog that extends Animal, including the required super() call.

config.intro: Follow `new Dog('Rex')` where Dog extends Animal.

steps.name: Call new Dog('Rex')
steps.detail: The engine begins constructing a new object whose prototype chain links Dog.prototype -> Animal.prototype.

steps.name: Enter Dog constructor
steps.detail: Before `this` is usable, the subclass must hand off to the parent.

steps.name: super('Rex') runs
steps.detail: Animal's constructor executes, setting this.name = 'Rex' on the new instance.

steps.name: Back in Dog constructor
steps.detail: Now `this` is initialized, so Dog can add its own fields (e.g. this.legs = 4).

steps.name: Return the instance
steps.detail: The finished object delegates to Dog.prototype for methods, then Animal.prototype.

steps.name: Call dog.speak()
steps.detail: Lookup finds speak on Dog.prototype (or via super) and runs it with this = dog.

debuggingLab.title: Using `this` before super()
debuggingLab.symptom: Constructing the subclass throws: ReferenceError: Must call super constructor before accessing 'this'.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: In a subclass constructor, `this` does not exist until super() runs the parent constructor and creates the instance. Touching this.breed before super(name) is a reference error. super() must be the first statement that initializes the object.
commonMistakes: Assuming this is available immediately in a subclass constructor.
Calling super() after setting subclass fields instead of before.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Reorder so the parent is initialized before the subclass adds its own fields.

theory.question: Are JavaScript classes real classes, or syntactic sugar?
theory.directAnswer: They're syntactic sugar over prototypes. A class is actually a function (typeof Class === 'function'), its methods live on Class.prototype, instances delegate to that prototype, and extends wires up the prototype chain. Classes just give a cleaner syntax for patterns you could write with constructor functions.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A readable syntax that compiles to constructor functions and prototype linkage.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Manual prototype wiring was verbose and error-prone, so ES2015 added class syntax for clarity while keeping the underlying model.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Methods are added to the prototype, the constructor initializes instance state, and extends sets the subclass prototype's [[Prototype]] to the parent's prototype.

theory.whyImportant: Knowing this prevents confusion about why method changes affect all instances and how instanceof works, and shows real understanding beyond surface syntax.
theory.realWorldExample: class Dog {} then Dog.prototype.bark = ... still works because the class is a constructor function with a prototype.

nestedTopics.title: Prototype methods
nestedTopics.explanation: Class methods are shared via the prototype, not copied per instance.

nestedTopics.title: Strict mode
nestedTopics.explanation: Class bodies always run in strict mode.

followUps.question: Where do class methods actually live?
followUps.answer: On the class's prototype object, so all instances share a single function reference.

followUps.question: Are class declarations hoisted?
followUps.answer: They're hoisted but stay in a temporal dead zone, so you can't use them before the declaration runs.

theory.question: How do private fields (#) differ from the underscore convention?
theory.directAnswer: An underscore prefix (_value) is private only by convention — the property is fully readable and writable from outside. A # field is enforced by the language: it's accessible only within the class body, isn't enumerable, and even attempting to access it from outside is a syntax error. # gives real encapsulation.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two approaches to privacy: a naming convention versus a language-enforced private slot.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Developers needed genuine encapsulation; the underscore was only a hint, so ES2022 added true private fields.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: # fields are stored in a hidden per-instance slot keyed by the private name, unreachable except through code lexically inside the class.

theory.whyImportant: Encapsulation prevents external code from depending on or corrupting internals, and interviewers test whether you know convention from enforcement.
theory.realWorldExample: A Wallet class with #balance can't have its balance set directly from outside, unlike _balance.

nestedTopics.title: Encapsulation
nestedTopics.explanation: Hiding internal state behind a controlled API.

nestedTopics.title: Getters/setters
nestedTopics.explanation: Expose private fields safely with validation.

followUps.question: Can subclasses access a parent's # fields?
followUps.answer: No — private fields are private to the declaring class, not inherited; subclasses can only use exposed methods or getters.

scenario.question: A subclass passes a class method as a callback (e.g. button.onClick = obj.handle) and inside it `this` is undefined. Why, and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: Class bodies run in strict mode, and when a method is detached and called as a plain function, `this` is undefined rather than the instance. Fix it by binding in the constructor (this.handle = this.handle.bind(this)), or by defining the method as an arrow-function class field (handle = () => {...}) which captures the instance's this.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A lost-this bug from passing a method without preserving its receiver.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Methods aren't bound to their instance; the value of this depends on how a function is called, and strict mode leaves it undefined for bare calls.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Binding or arrow class fields fix this to the instance permanently regardless of how the function is later invoked.

scenario.whyImportant: It's an extremely common React/event-handler bug and a frequent interview question about this-binding.

nestedTopics.title: this binding
nestedTopics.explanation: this depends on the call site unless bound.

followUps.question: What's the tradeoff of arrow class fields?
followUps.answer: They create a new function per instance (more memory) and live on the instance, not the prototype, so they're not shared.

coding.question: Implement a class hierarchy: a Shape base with area(), and Circle and Rectangle subclasses that override it. Add a static method that returns the largest shape from a list.
coding.thoughtProcess: I'll make Shape define a default area() (or throw), then override area() in each subclass using their own fields. A static method on Shape can iterate a list and use polymorphic area() to find the max, since static methods belong to the class and don't need an instance.
coding.lineByLine: Shape.area returns a default; subclasses override it with their own formulas using fields set after super(). Shape.largest is static, so it's called as Shape.largest(list); reduce compares shapes by their polymorphic area() and returns the bigger one — demonstrating overriding plus static methods.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) for largest over n shapes.

alternativeApproaches.title: Abstract base via throw
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Make Shape.area throw to force subclasses to implement it, emulating an abstract method.

followUps.question: Why must subclass constructors call super() before using this?
followUps.answer: The parent constructor creates and initializes the instance; this isn't available until super() runs.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Classes structure domain models and services in OOP-style code: entities with shared methods, inheritance for shared behavior, and encapsulation via private fields. Many frameworks expose base classes (e.g., custom Error subtypes) you extend.
productionDeepDive.performance: Methods live on the prototype and are shared, keeping instances lightweight. Arrow-function class fields trade memory (one function per instance) for stable this-binding; consistent shapes and # fields keep engines optimized.
productionDeepDive.security: Private # fields enforce encapsulation, preventing external code from reading or mutating sensitive internals like tokens or balances — stronger than underscore conventions which are trivially bypassed.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Shared prototype methods scale well across many instances. Deep inheritance hierarchies become rigid and hard to change; prefer composition or mixins as systems grow.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Classes make intent clear for entity modeling, but overusing inheritance creates fragile base-class problems. Keep hierarchies shallow and favor small, focused classes.
productionDeepDive.observability: instanceof and class names aid debugging and logging; custom error classes (extends Error) give meaningful stack traces and let you branch on error type in monitoring.

caseStudies.problem: Need extensible, typed building blocks (components, errors, services).
caseStudies.solution: Expose base classes consumers extend (e.g. extends Error, extends Component).
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Inheritance coupling vs. familiar, structured extension points.
caseStudies.lessons: Use classes for clear entity/error modeling; prefer composition over deep hierarchies.

A balance getter exposing the private field read-only

How do private # fields improve safety over a _balance convention here?

keyTakeaways: A class is a template for objects; the constructor initializes instance data and methods are shared via the prototype.
extends + super set up inheritance; super() must run before using `this` in a subclass constructor.
static members belong to the class itself; getters/setters expose computed or validated properties.
Private # fields give language-enforced encapsulation, unlike the underscore convention.
Classes are syntactic sugar over prototypes — typeof Class is 'function' and instanceof walks the prototype chain.
